en: On the day of Yichou in the second month of the tenth year of the Chunxi era,

by Imperial Decree, one copy of the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* (The Great Perfect Enlightenment Sutra) with the Imperial Commentary was bestowed upon this subject, Bao Yin. [I, the subject] prostrate nine times and humbly read it while burning incense, as if in the presence of the Divine Spirit.
I, Shan, have personally heard this; there is not the slightest discrepancy. (Your servant) respectfully submits this memorial to express my gratitude.

I further present this verse in praise of Your Majesty’s sacred virtue, requesting that it be carved into woodblocks at Mount Jing to circulate throughout the four quarters, so that the monastics of the empire may illuminate their own minds and together ferry across the Great Perfect Enlightenment Sea of the Tathāgata.
Having received the gracious imperial decree granting this request, (Your servant) respectfully prostrates himself with his head to the ground.
The statement says: "The self-nature of perfect enlightenment is not a nature" is a direct pointing. That "the Sage speaks though there is nothing to speak of" is an expedient means.
Throughout all Buddhas in the Great Treasury of Radiance, they abide in majestic radiance; this is precisely the pure enlightened mind of all sentient beings.
At this time, the preaching and listening were complete, and the meaning of the Dharma was fully established.

Then the Bhagavān, in response to Mañjuśrī, declared that the original existence of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna*) and the original emptiness of ignorance (*avidyā*) constitute the primary cause for the practice of the Dharma.

This was intended to free sentient beings from false views; thus, he directly pointed to the root source, wherein there are no further branches or leaves. For the sake of all beings, Samantabhadra and the other great Bodhisattvas...
Therefore, where there is no room for doubt, various doubts arise; yet the Tathāgata, according to each individual's capacity, is able to respond in manifold ways where there is no need for response.
This is like how a capital city is not entered through only one gate, nor is a great mansion supported by only one beam.

This is called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*); there is nothing that is not perfectly enlightened. This is called the Definitive Meaning (*nītārtha*); there is nothing that is not definitively understood. Thus, [the twelve]...
That which is collectively elucidated by all the various scriptures takes this as their eyes; that which was transmitted solely by the thirty-five patriarchs takes this as their marrow.
(Your servant) the fool says: one who is fully endowed with perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) yet dwells within it is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
one who is perfect enlightenment all day long yet has never experienced it is a Tathāgata. Although [this is] with Pei...
The views of Xiu and [my] own regarding the signs of realization are as opposed as ice and charcoal; only one who has attained direct personal verification can truly know this.
I reverently consider Your Majesty, the Present Emperor: you have attained the Dharma of the Buddha-mind, which is vast and all-pervasive, numinous and brilliantly penetrating.

Your benevolence is like Heaven, your wisdom is like the spirit, and you are a Sage in stillness and a King in action. Is this not indeed the wondrous function of the single mind of Perfect Enlightenment?

In the leisure between the myriad affairs of state, he sported within the Great Treasury of Radiance (*Mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*). Taking up his brush, he composed this work to manifest and propagate the Sage’s intent.
Indeed, it is because the Way of every Buddha is the same; though not spoken, it is spoken through words that point directly to the truth.
(Your servant) respectfully examines that since the Buddha-dharma flowed into China, it has been...
The Emperor Taizong Wenhuang of the Tang dynasty personally composed a preface for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, placing it at its head, yet he never provided a commentary upon it.

Now, our present Emperor, Your Majesty, has revealed the Dharma of the One Mind by composing a commentary on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (The Great Perfect Enlightenment) to awaken the multitude of deluded beings. This is truly...

He stands at the pinnacle of a hundred sovereigns; he alone surpasses all predecessors. Formerly, Chan Master Zongmi of Mount Guifeng appended commentaries to this work, yet its text was vast and prolix.

Now, Your Majesty’s commentary is concise in expression yet rich in meaning, succinct in phrasing yet exhaustive in principle. Since the time of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng), there has been none like it.
For indeed, this book has never existed before. I, your servant,
respectfully take this imperial copy to carve it into printing blocks so that it may be transmitted without end,
thereby perpetuating the ancestral sacrifices.

May the holy longevity of the two palaces be boundless. May this further bring blessings equally to the four seas, so that all who see or hear of it may realize that what is illusory is to be detached from, and that detachment from illusion is awakening.
Through such enlightenment, may they forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra. This is but a tiny fraction of my humble response to the glorious mandate.
The Dharma-transmitting (Subject) Monk (Bao Yin), Abbot of Xingsheng Wanshou Chan Temple at Jingshan in Lin’an Prefecture, prostrates himself with joined palms and respectfully states:
[Verse] The Buddhas of antiquity and the Buddhas of today Share one and the same broad and long tongue; Within that which has no tracks or paths...
Opening a path for all beings, He parts the clouds of a thousand obstructions;

Releasing a single moon across the heavens, He causes all people on earth To attain complete clarity beneath his words. Awakening is nothing to be perfected, And illusion is nothing to be extinguished;
In this very absence of even "non-existence," Is a single snowflake upon a red-hot furnace.
I prostrate to the Buddhas and the Buddha— In every word, there is no divergent teaching.
*Imperial Commentary on the Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment, Explaining its Definitive Meaning*, Volume One.

[Regarding the title: "Great Vaipulya" (*Mahāvaipulya*) refers to a vastness that is immeasurable and boundless. This is because the essential nature of Perfect Enlightenment pervades the entire Dharma-realm, just as the vastness of a great square space. "Perfect" (*yuan*) means complete and fully endowed; "Enlightenment" (*jue*) means empty clarity and spiritual illumination. [The text continues with] "Cultivation" (*xiu*).

Regarding the term *tāra*, according to various commentaries, it is a general designation for all sūtras; as for "sūtra of definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*), it praises this particular sūtra as having the sense of ultimate and thorough realization.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Buddhatoṭara of Kapiśā during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard (Ānanda said: "This scriptural teaching was personally heard from the Buddha").

At one time (when the Buddha spoke this sūtra), the Bhagavān (the *Bhagavat* is an alternative title for the Buddha according to the Tripiṭaka) entered the Great Treasury of Supernatural Powers and Radiance (the Buddha enters a great samādhi; because his supernatural powers and radiance are inexhaustible, it is called a "treasury"). 3.

Entering into samādhi (*samāpatti*). (Regarding *samādhi*: it is the wondrous state spontaneously attained within right concentration. Regarding *samāpatti*: it is called "right reception" because one does not receive any [sensory] receptions. All Tathāgatas. (The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:)

The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. He is the Abiding Sustenance of Radiant Adornment (Guangyan). "Radiant Adornment" means adornment by light. "Abiding" means abiding without remaining fixed.

"Sustaining" means receiving and upholding without loss. This is the ground of pure awakening for all sentient beings. (Because Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally of one nature, the place where the Buddhas abide as radiant adornment is precisely the ground of the pure awakening mind of sentient beings.

It is the limit of original reality where body and mind are quiescent and equal. (Once quiescence is realized, the essence of the holy and the ordinary is identical; only then does one see the original true limit, wherein no distinctions or inequalities exist. Perfect.

Filling the ten directions (because the nature of awakening is perfect and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm). Accordant with non-duality (though conforming to all conditions, the nature of awakening remains eternally one).

Within the realm of non-duality, he manifests various pure lands (within the single nature of the Buddha, which is called the realm of non-duality, he transforms and guides sentient beings through dharmas that are unattached and unstained).
He was accompanied by one hundred thousand great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Their names were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva,
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Viśuddhamati Bodhisattva, Vaśitāprāpta Bodhisattva,
Gadgadasvara Bodhisattva, Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhana Bodhisattva, Samantabodhi Bodhisattva, Pariniṣpannabodhi Bodhisattva, and Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva.
...and so forth, acting as the leaders. Together with their retinues, they all entered into samādhi and dwelt together in the Tathāgata’s assembly of the equal Dharma.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Having circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right, he knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, we pray that you will, for the sake of all the members of this assembly who have come as Dharma-folk, expound upon the Tathāgata’s original arising of pure practice on the causal ground (where 'original arising' refers to the first mind initially aroused by the Buddha when he was an ordinary person;

'causal ground' refers to the Buddha's first stage; and 'Dharma-practice' refers to the Buddha's wondrous conduct). Furthermore, please expound upon how Bodhisattvas give rise to purity within the Mahāyāna."

With a pure mind, he remained free from all ailments (all ailments being various illusions). He was able to ensure that sentient beings of future末代 times who seek the Mahāyāna would not fall into false views.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground (the five limbs being the head and the four extremities).
He made this request three times, beginning again at the end of each cycle (three requests being the ultimate form of reverence).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

It is well that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the practices for attaining the Way on the causal ground for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age who seek the Mahāyāna, so that they may attain correct sustenance and not fall into false views. Listen attentively now; I shall [explain]..."
"I shall speak for you. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

"Good son, there is the Unsurpassed Dharma King (a title of the Buddha; for the Buddha has awakened to the Supreme Vehicle and is the sovereign of all phenomena, as there is nothing higher than him)."

The Great Dharani Gate is named Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). (Regarding the "Dharani Gate," the Tripitaka states it is the "Gate of Total Retention" [*dhāraṇī*]. Here, Perfect Enlightenment is designated as the Great Dharani Gate.)

This is because it comprehensively encompasses the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates. It flows forth from all pure *tathatā* (this refers to the wondrous nature of true emptiness, which is suchness and immovable;

Pei Xiu also said that because it is non-deceptive and unchanging, it is called *tathatā*). *Bodhi* (translated as "Awakening"; the Sixth Patriarch said: "If the preceding thought clings to objects, it is affliction;

if the succeeding thought is detached from objects, it is *bodhi*. What else could it be but awakening?"). *Nirvāṇa* (translated as "Quiescent Extinction"). And the *pāramitās* (translated as "Reaching the Other Shore," or "The Culmination of Affairs"). Teaching and instructing the bodhisattvas (the Buddha’s transmission of instruction).

This is for the sake of instructing all Bodhisattvas. The original ground where all Tathāgatas first established their practice was entirely based upon the aspect of perfectly illuminating, pure awakening (*vimala-bodhi-lakṣaṇa*).

("Entirely based upon" means "entirely caused by. "Perfectly illuminating" means perfect clarity and tranquil illumination. "Pure" means unstained by anything. "Aspect of awakening" refers to the aspect of non-aspect. As Master Fu said: "To have a body is not the essence of awakening; formlessness is the true form.")
Only by permanently severing ignorance can one achieve the Buddha-way.
What is ignorance? (Sentient beings, through delusive conceptualization, lose sight of the nature of true awakening and clarity; therefore, it is called ignorance.

Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have undergone various inversions, just as a person who has lost their way mistakes the four directions for one another. (Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have taken the delusive as...)

Truly so. It is like a person who has lost their way and cannot determine the fixed directions of east, west, south, or north. They falsely identify the four great elements as the characteristics of their own body (the illusory form composed of the provisional union of earth, water, fire, and wind;

sentient beings, through inversion, take this to be the true characteristic of the self). They take the shadows of the conditions of the six sense objects as the characteristics of their own mind (the shadows of the six kinds of objective conditions: form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena).
Sentient beings are inverted; they take what is the true reality of their own minds to be something else.

For example, it is like those with diseased eyes who see flowers in the sky or a second moon (falsely identifying the characteristics of the body and the mind, just as one with cataracts falsely sees flowers in the sky, or one who presses on the eye falsely sees two moons). Good son, in emptiness there are truly no flowers; it is only the sick person who falsely clings to them.

All illusions are fundamentally empty; sentient beings delusively perceive them as existent, just as those with cataracts falsely cling to the existence of flowers in the sky that are originally non-existent.

Because of this false clinging, they are not only deluded regarding the self-nature of this empty space, but are also confused about the source from which those real flowers arise. (Sentient beings, due to false clinging, are not only deluded concerning their own nature of emptiness, but furthermore do not know that the cataract in the eye is actually the source from which the flowers in the sky arise.
Because of this, they falsely undergo the cycle of birth and death; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). Because of this...
Through various inversions, one thus falsely experiences the cycle of birth and death. In reality, there is no such cycle of birth and death; therefore, it is said that they "falsely exist.
Good son, this ignorance has no real substance. (Ignorance arises from delusion; it possesses no real essence or characteristic. It is like a person in a dream:
while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon waking, nothing is found. (This explains that when sentient beings are deluded, they take ignorance to be profoundly real, but upon awakening...)

Only afterwards does one come to know that ignorance is an illusion. It is like various empty flowers vanishing into space; one cannot say there is a fixed place where they cease. Why? Because they have no place of birth.
(The cessation of ignorance is like the cessation of empty flowers; that one cannot point to a place of cessation is because ignorance fundamentally has no place of birth.)
All sentient beings falsely perceive arising and ceasing within that which is non-arising; therefore, it is called "revolving in birth and death.

(Sentient beings falsely perceive the illusory body as having the characteristics of arising and ceasing; therefore, the Buddha calls it "revolving in birth and death. To say it is "called" [thus] means it does not truly exist.)
Good son, when a Tathāgata cultivates Perfect Enlightenment on the causal ground, he knows that these are like flowers in the sky, and thus there is no cyclic existence.

(For one first cultivating Perfect Enlightenment, he knows that the marks of arising and ceasing are like those flowers in the sky; as arising and ceasing are suddenly empty, there is no cyclic existence. Furthermore, there is no body or mind that undergoes birth and death. (Since there is no cyclic existence...)

Body and mind are also empty. Since body and mind are empty, where can birth and death reside? They do not exist because they are uncreated; they do not exist because their fundamental nature is non-existent (it is not that they become non-existent through some act of creation, for their nature is fundamentally pure and non-existent).

That which perceives is like empty space. (When cognition arises within awakening, that which is perceived is likewise illusory; as in that empty space, it is understood to be not the Buddha-nature. That which knows empty space—

This is precisely the appearance of empty flowers (when the mind clings to stubborn emptiness, it reverts to the appearance of form). Nor can it be said that there is no nature of awareness (lest one give rise to thoughts of nihilistic annihilation).

When both existence and non-existence are cast aside, this is called "conformity with pure awakening" (having neither knowledge nor ignorance, being unattached to either; thus it is said that both existence and non-existence are cast aside.

As for "conformity with pure awakening," the nature of awakening is pure and does not establish a mark of self; therefore, it can conform to all things without deluded attachment, just as Confucius’s "extinguishing the four [extremes]"). Why is this? Because the nature of space...

Therefore, it is eternally unmoving (for its nature is like empty space, and it is because one constantly does not stir the mind). Within the Tathāgatagarbha there is neither arising nor ceasing, and there is neither cognition nor vision (the Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the nature of pure awakening;

within the nature of pure awakening, there are fundamentally no marks of birth and death, and fundamentally no establishment of cognition or vision). It is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm.

(The essence of the nature of Perfect Enlightenment is as vast as the Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said to be "like the nature of the Dharma-realm. It is ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions; thus, all virtues are fully endowed within it, without limit or boundary.
This is what is called the practice of the Dharma on the causal ground. By means of this, Bodhisattvas give rise to the pure mind within the Mahāyāna.
Sentient beings of the final age who rely on this for cultivation will not fall into false views.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Mañjuśrī, you should know: All Tathāgatas, from their original ground of practice, Awakened through wisdom And fully understood ignorance; They knew it to be like flowers in the sky."
One is then able to escape the cycle of transmigration. Furthermore, like one within a dream, upon waking, the dreamer cannot be found;
awakening is like space— equanimous and unmoving. When awakening pervades the ten directions, one immediately attains the Way of the Buddha.
Where all illusions cease to exist, even the attainment of Buddhahood is ungraspable.
Because its fundamental nature is perfect, within this, the Bodhisattva is able to give rise to the bodhicitta;
sentient beings of the final age who practice this will escape false views.
Thereupon, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him to the right.
He circumambulated [the Buddha] three times, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas in this gathering, and for all sentient beings of the future age who practice the Mahāyāna, having heard of this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment, how should they cultivate it?
World-Honored One, if those sentient beings know that which is like an illusion, then their bodies and minds are also illusions."

"How is it that one uses illusion to cultivate illusion? (Since one knows that all things are like illusions, then body and mind are also illusions. For what reason, then, does one use this illusory body and illusory mind to cultivate those illusory dharmas?

If the nature of all illusions were completely extinguished, then there would be no mind; who would be the one to practice cultivation? Why, then, do you further say that cultivation is like an illusion?

(If the natures of all illusions were extinguished, then there would be a state of profound stillness without mind, and likewise no person to perform the cultivation. Since their nature cannot be extinguished, then cultivation is not an illusion. For what reason, then..."*
This refers to practicing according to the nature of illusion (the intended meaning of this Bodhisattva’s question).

If sentient beings do not fundamentally practice, they will perpetually dwell within birth and death as mere illusions and transformations, never understanding the illusory nature of reality. How, then, can their deluded minds be liberated?

(If one claims that cultivation is unnecessary from the outset, then one would eternally remain within illusion, failing to comprehend the illusory realm; by what means, then, could their deluded minds be liberated? I pray that you will act as a guide for all sentient beings of the final age.

"What skillful means and gradual cultivation should be practiced to cause all sentient beings to forever leave behind all illusions? Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
Thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to cultivate the illusory-like samādhi of a bodhisattva through skillful means and gradual stages, so as to enable all sentient beings to become free from all illusions. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you. At that time, Samantabhadra...
The virtuous Bodhisattva, having received these instructions, rejoiced; together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.
"Good son, the various illusory manifestations of all sentient beings all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha-citta*).

They are like flowers in the sky that appear from space itself. Although the illusory flowers perish, the nature of space is not destroyed. (While the wondrous mind is not yet clarified, the various illusions compete to arise. For example,)"
Flowers in the sky arise from the void; when they vanish through illusion, the wondrous mind alone remains (just as when flowers perish, the nature of the void is not diminished).

The illusory minds of sentient beings likewise depend upon the cessation of illusion (for that illusory mind arises because of illusion, and only through illusory wisdom can it be extinguished). When all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind is unmoving (when all illusions are entirely extinguished, the fundamental nature of Perfect Enlightenment has never moved).

To speak of awakening based on illusion is also called illusion (to speak of awakening while remaining within illusion—even speaking based on illusion—it is therefore appropriate to call it illusion). If one says there is...

Awakening is still not free from illusion; the same applies to speaking of non-awakening. (The original nature of awakening does not belong to existence or non-existence; if one speaks of existence or non-existence, one has not yet escaped illusion.
Therefore, the extinction of illusion is called immovability. (After the extinction of illusion, the nature of awakening is suchness.)
Good son, all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should distance themselves from all illusory and false realms.

This is because they maintain a mind of resolute detachment. (To distance oneself from all illusory realms is fundamentally due to maintaining a firm resolve that there shall forever be no illusory mind.

One should likewise distance oneself from the mind that is like an illusion. (If one’s numinous mind is like an illusory transformation, it too should be distanced; one must not cling to it. Distance yourself.

It is an illusion, and it should also be relinquished. (The mind that seeks to relinquish all illusions is itself an illusion; it too should be relinquished. One relinquishes even the relinquishing of illusions, and this too is relinquished.
(The desire to cast off the mind of relinquishment is itself an illusion; it too should be relinquished. When there is nothing further to relinquish, all illusions are eliminated.

(When one has completely relinquished every illusory mind, then illusion has no place to abide. It is like drilling for fire by means of two pieces of wood: when the fire emerges, the wood is exhausted and the ashes fly away while the smoke vanishes. By means of illusion...

The cultivation of illusion is also like this. Although all illusions are exhausted, they do not enter into annihilation. (It is like drilling wood to produce fire: the wood is consumed by the fire; when both the wood and the fire are gone...)

Only the ground remains. It is like using an illusory mind to further cultivate illusory dharmas; when all illusions are extinguished, the awakened nature remains ever-present). Good son, to know illusion is to be detached from it;

no expedient means are required (if the mind knows something is an illusion, one should immediately distance oneself from it—why rely on expedients?). To be detached from illusion is awakening; there is also no gradual progression (to completely detach from all illusions is itself true awakening;

one suddenly realizes the original mind, with no further stages). All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should practice according to this; only in this way can they [attain realization].
Forever free from all illusions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Samantabhadra, you should know: All sentient beings, Since beginningless time, have been subject to illusory ignorance."
All arise from the Tathāgatas, established within the mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
They are like flowers in the sky that appear based upon space; if these sky-flowers were to vanish, space itself remains fundamentally unmoving.
Illusion arises from various states of awakening; when illusion ceases, awakening is perfected. This is because the mind of awakening is immovable.
If those bodhisattvas, as well as sentient beings of the final age, always distance themselves from illusions, they will be entirely free from all illusions.
Just as fire arises within wood and the fire is extinguished when the wood is exhausted, awakening has no gradual stages;
skillful means are likewise thus.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas in this gathering, and for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age, we pray that you will expound the gradual stages of a bodhisattva’s practice. How is this so?”

Contemplation: (How should one contemplate so as to constitute right mindfulness? Sustaining: (How should one sustain [the practice] so as to achieve non-loss? Regarding sentient beings who have not yet awakened: what skillful means should be employed to cause them all to attain awakening?
(This is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which seeks to cause sentient beings to "open, show, awaken, and enter"; here, one asks what skillful means should be practiced.

World-Honored One, if those sentient beings lack right skillful means and right contemplation—(in the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras*, not falling into the unconditioned is taken as right skillful means, and severing deluded thoughts is taken as right contemplation; today we say they lack these)—[how can they be saved?]
"Expedient means" refers to falling into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). One who lacks right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) does not sever deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).

Upon hearing the Buddha, the Tathāgata, speak of this samādhi, their minds become confused and distressed, and they are unable to enter into the realization of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). We pray that you will arouse compassion for our kind and for sentient beings of the末法 (final dharma) age, and provisionally explain expedient means.

(The previous chapter stated that "knowing illusion is itself detachment, requiring no further expedient means. Because sentient beings have not yet realized this, Samantacakṣus requests the Buddha to provisionally explain expedient means. Thus it was done.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again from the end.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

Son of good family, you are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the gradual stages of cultivation and contemplation."
"Abiding in the maintenance [of the Dharma], and even employing various provisional skillful means, listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.

"Good son, those newly initiated bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect awakened mind should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions.
(Right mindfulness is non-mindfulness. When there is no thought of anything at all, all illusions naturally recede. Those who cultivate perfect awakening should act in this way.)"

First, rely upon the practice of *śamatha* (translated as "cessation," which is concentration). As the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "The practitioner of *śamatha* takes ultimate stillness as their practice.

Firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*)—all prohibitive precepts should be firmly upheld, for it is through the precepts that one enters concentration—and dwell peacefully among your followers (ensuring my followers all dwell in peace, so that my mind is free from affliction and I may cultivate the Way).
Seated in quietude within a silent chamber, constantly maintain this thought: "This body of mine is now a composite of the four great elements. (Seated in quietude, in a single...)

At all times, one should constantly reflect within oneself: "This present illusory body of mine exists through the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind. That is to say, the hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities—all these material forms return to earth.
Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, spittle, foam, phlegm, tears, vital essence, and the excretions of both large and small—these all return to water.
The warmth returns to fire, and movement returns to wind. Thus, the four great elements each [dissolve into their own source]."

[The mind] departs. Now, where should this delusory body be? (Reflecting thus upon the four great elements, each returning to its source, one considers: where should this present illusory body be? One immediately realizes that this body ultimately has no substance;

it exists as a manifestation of conjunction, truly identical to a magical creation. (Only after the four great elements have dispersed and ceased does one know that the illusory body was originally empty—that it was a form provisionally formed through combination, truly identical to a magical creation.

This is precisely what Liezi meant when he said that the puppet crafted by the master puppeteer excels in song and dance, yet when dissected, it is merely made of leather and wood. This refers exactly to that.

Through the provisional conjunction of four conditions, the six sense organs falsely arise. (The "four conditions" refer to the four great elements. The six sense organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally (within are the four great elements; without are the six sense organs; through their internal and external provisional conjunction, this illusory body is formed). Through delusion, there arises the breath of conditions.

Within this, they accumulate. (As for "conditioning-energies," these are false form and mind that manifest from conditions. "Accumulating within" means they gather and do not disperse within the illusory body).

They appear to have the marks of conditions and are conventionally designated as "mind. (Conditioning-energies accumulate within; the marks of conditions take shape without. "Appearing to exist" means these marks are not actually present. "Conventionally designated" means this mind is not truly existent).

Good son, this false mind cannot exist if the six sense objects are absent. (If there were no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, all false minds would likewise cease to exist.)

When the six kinds of illusory objects entice from without, from where does this mind arise? When the four great elements are analyzed and dispersed, no object can be found. At the time when the four great elements perish, the various objects that cause defilement—
Not a single speck of dust can be found there to exist. Within this, the objects of perception each dissolve and vanish; ultimately, no perceiving mind can be seen.
(After the four conditions and six sense-objects have dissolved and vanished, that which is called the "perceiving mind" is utterly invisible.)
Good son, for those sentient beings, because the illusory body ceases, the illusory mind also ceases; because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease.

(Since the illusory body has ceased, the illusory mind has nothing upon which to rely, and thus it disperses and ceases. Since the illusory mind has ceased, there is no one to be stained by or attached to the illusory objects, and thus they also disperse and cease.

Because the illusory objects cease, the cessation of illusion also ceases. (Since the illusory objects have ceased, all illusions are entirely empty; even the trace of the cessation of illusion is likewise non-existent. Because the cessation of illusion ceases, it is not...

Illusions do not cease [in themselves]. (When all illusions are extinguished, even the extinction of illusion ceases. The awakened nature is not an illusion; it never undergoes cessation. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is gone, the clarity appears. (The mirror is a metaphor for the fundamental nature;

the grime is a metaphor for the various illusions. When the grime is gone and clarity appears, when illusions are exhausted, the nature is luminous. Good son, you should know that both body and mind are entirely illusory grime. (The illusory body and the illusory mind.)

The obstructions to my enlightened nature are like filth defiling a pure object. Once the characteristics of defilement are eternally extinguished, the ten directions become pure. Since the characteristics of defilement in body and mind have been eternally extinguished, throughout the ten directions...
Pure and unstained).
Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel which, when reflected by the five colors, manifests each according to its direction.

(The *Yuanjue chao* states: "In Sanskrit, 'maṇi' means 'wish-fulfilling jewel. The substance of the jewel is luminous and pure; it reflects the colors of the five directions. Thus, the mind of Perfect Enlightenment is tranquil and pure, manifesting in response throughout the ten directions. All those who are ignorant...

One sees that those mani-jewels truly possess five colors. (The foolish do not know that the essence of the jewel is luminous and pure, reflecting the five colors; they instead claim that the five colors truly exist within the jewel.

This is just as sentient beings claim that the Buddha truly possesses physical form. Good son, the pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment manifests within body and mind, responding to each according to its kind.
(The pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment manifests bodies and minds, appearing in response to each and every class of sentient beings, just as with the thirty-two transformations of Avalokiteśvara.

Those who are deluded likewise claim that within the pure, perfect enlightenment there truly exist such self-characteristics of body and mind. this may be called true delusion. Because of this, they cannot distance themselves from illusory transformations. (Sentient beings...)

"Because of this deluded attachment, one is unable to distance oneself from all illusions. Therefore, I say that body and mind are illusory defilements (since the Buddha spoke of them as 'illusory defilements' due to that deluded attachment to body and mind)."

In relation to being free from the defilement of illusion, one is called a "Bodhisattva. (This means that for one who has awakened to and eliminated illusion—just as medicine is prescribed for an illness—the Buddha says that such a person who possesses the awakening that can eliminate the defilement of illusion is named a Bodhisattva.

When the defilements are exhausted (the illusory defilements of body and mind are all eternally extinguished), and when there is no longer any opposition (even the awakening that opposes illusion no longer exists), then there is no opposition to defilement (for one who opposes illusion, there is also no illusory defilement).

Furthermore, regarding the designation "one who is so named" (to say "Bodhisattva" is also an illusory name; since both [subject and object] are now empty in relation to defilement, how could this characteristic of a Bodhisattva exist?). Well done.

"Good man, because these bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age have realized that all illusions are extinguished as images, they then attain pure non-directionality (at that time, all illusory images are extinguished, and they immediately attain pure non-directionality; 'non-directional' means not being restricted by spatial location).
Boundless empty space is manifested by awakening (having attained pure non-directionality, then boundless empty space is revealed through awakening)."
Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the purity of the mind is revealed. Because the mind is pure, the objects of perception are seen as pure.
Because the seeing is pure, the eye-faculty is pure. Because the faculty is pure, the eye-consciousness is pure.

Whatever one desires to see is entirely a defiled thought; therefore, it is called "seeing dust. The eye is the fundamental source of seeing; therefore, it is called the "eye-faculty" (*cakṣur-indriya*). The eye is able to differentiate various forms; therefore, it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣur-vijñāna*). Because consciousness is pure, the dust of sound is pure.
Because hearing is pure, the ear-faculty is pure. Because the faculty is pure, ear-consciousness is pure.

Whatever one desires to hear is entirely a thought of sensory dust; therefore, it is called "hearing-dust. Because the ear is the fundamental source of hearing, it is called the "ear-faculty" (*śrotrendriya*). Because the ear can differentiate various sounds, it is called "ear-consciousness" (*śrotravijñāna*).
Because consciousness is pure, the objects of perception (*viṣaya*) are pure. This applies likewise to the nose, tongue, body, and mind. Whatever the mind perceives is also a thought of sensory dust.

Therefore it is said: "One awakens to the fact that the nose, tongue, body, and mind each have their respective objects, faculties, and consciousnesses; all these become pure because the self-mind is pure.
Good son, because the faculties are pure, the object of form is pure; because form is pure, the object of sound is pure; and the same applies to the objects of fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas.

(When the six sense organs are already purified, then the six kinds of illusory objects—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—are also all purified. Good son, because the six objects are purified, the earth element is greatly purified;
because the earth element is purified, the water element is greatly purified; the fire element and the wind element are likewise so.

(Since the six objects are already purified, the four great elements—the false conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind—are also all purified. Good son, because the four great elements are purified, the twelve bases...

The six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), combined, constitute the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). The six sense organs are: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The six sense objects are: form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharma*). The eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"These are the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six types of discerning consciousness. The purity of the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). The *Zhuangchun Lu* states: "Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are twenty-five kinds of existence. Those termed the four continents are:

Pūrvavideha (Eastern Victory Body Continent), Aparagodānīya (Western Cow-Product Continent), Jambudvīpa (Southern Rose-Apple Continent), and Uttarakuru (Northern Kurus Continent). The six heavens of the desire realm are: Cāturmahārājika (Four Heavenly Kings), Trāyastriṃśa (Heaven of the Thirty-three), Yāma (Yama Heaven), Tuṣita (Tuṣita Heaven)..."

The Nirmāṇarati Heaven and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the four evil destinies—namely, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras; the four dhyāna heavens—namely, the first dhyāna heaven, the second dhyāna heaven, the third dhyāna heaven, and the fourth dhyāna heaven;

and the four formless heavens—namely, the Ākāśānantyāyatana heaven, the Vijñānānantyāyatana heaven, the Ākiṃcanyāyatana heaven, and the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana heaven. Furthermore, there is one Brahmakāyika heaven, one Asaṃjñisattva heaven, and the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, totaling twenty-five types of existence (*bhava*).

They are collectively termed "existence" because they all belong to the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*). Now, by virtue of the purity of one's own mind, all these become pure. Because they are pure, the Ten Powers...

(The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: 1. The power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; 2. The power of knowing the retribution of karma throughout the three periods of time; 3. The power of knowing all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis; 4. The power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of beings;

5. The power of knowing the various inclinations of sentient beings; 6. The power of knowing the various dispositions of the world; 7. The power of knowing the attainment of all paths; 8. The power of recollecting past lives; 9. The power of the divine eye that can perceive all things; 10.

The power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. The four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). (The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: 1. Fearlessness regarding omniscience; 2. Fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; 3. Fearlessness regarding the teaching of obstacles to the path; 4. Fearlessness regarding the teaching of the path to the end of suffering. The four unimpeded knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

(1) Unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); 2) unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); 3) unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); 4) unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* states: "Unimpeded knowledge of meaning refers to the attainment of the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Unimpeded knowledge of phenomena refers to understanding all phenomena as they truly are. Unimpeded knowledge of expression refers to various analytical distinctions through skillful speech. Unimpeded knowledge of eloquence refers to preaching according to the capacities of beings, without conceiving of dualistic characteristics.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). The *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "1) No error; 2) No harsh or abrupt speech; 3) No loss of mindfulness; 4) No unconcentrated mind; 5) No perception of diversity; 6) No equanimity lacking discernment; 7) No deficiency in aspiration..."

1. Non-retrogression; 2. Non-retrogression in vigor; 3. Non-retrogression in mindfulness; 4. Non-retrogression in wisdom (*prajñā*); 5. Non-retrogression in liberation (*vimukti*); 6. Non-retrogression in the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*); 7. Regarding that knowledge and vision, there is no attachment and no obstruction concerning the past.

14. Whether it be knowledge or vision, it is unattached and unimpeded regarding the present world. 15. Whether it be knowledge or vision, it is unattached and unimpeded regarding the future world. 16. All bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and proceed in accordance with knowledge.

17. All verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. 18. All mental actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. These are the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) of a Buddha. "Unique" means that only a Buddha alone possesses them;

they are not shared with the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are pure. As the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—these together constitute the thirty-seven factors.

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness: contemplating the body as impure, contemplating feelings as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as non-self. Regarding the four right efforts: the faculty of diligence.

The awakening factor of energy, the power of energy, right effort, and the four bases of psychic power consist of: the faculty of concentration, the awakening factor of concentration, the power of concentration, and right concentration. The five faculties are: the faculty of faith, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of energy, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. The five powers are: the power of faith, the power of mindfulness, [the power of energy, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom].

The power of diligence, the power of wisdom, the power of concentration; the seven factors of enlightenment—namely, the factor of mindfulness, the factor of investigation of phenomena, the factor of diligence, the factor of joy, the factor of tranquility, the factor of concentration, and the factor of equanimity;
and the eight branches of the noble path—namely, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, and right view.

In this manner, up to the eighty-four thousand gates of *dhāraṇī*, all are completely pure. (The Tripitaka states: "Gates of *dhāraṇī*" refers to the gates of total retention. Since sentient beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions, there are eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates. Now, because one's own mind is pure and utterly transcends affliction, these Dharma-gates are all...)

All are pure). Good son, because the nature of all real marks (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is pure, the single body is pure. (The "nature of real marks" refers to the fact that the nature of the previously mentioned sense bases, objects, four great elements, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment exists as it truly is;

thus it is called the "nature of real marks. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "That which is the real mark is precisely the absence of marks. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'real mark. This is what is meant by these natures.)
Being pure and unstained, the single true *dharmakāya* is entirely pure. Because one body is pure, many bodies are pure; since the single true *dharmakāya* is already pure...

All transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are likewise pure. As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "The Buddha’s transformation bodies travel everywhere to buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all are the Buddha-body. Is this not the case that if one body is pure, then many bodies are pure?

Because many bodies are pure, it extends in this way even to the sentient beings of the ten directions, whose *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti* (perfectly realized awakening) is pure. Because many bodies are pure, one universally contemplates the nature of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and finds them all to be thus pure in their *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti*.

The *Commentary on the Perfect Awakening* (*Yuánjué shù*) also says: "This means that when one person awakens to their own nature, they know that the fundamental nature of all sentient beings is pure; it does not mean that one person practices the Way while many [others do not]."
[He] attains Buddhahood). Good son, because one world is pure, many worlds are pure. (Since one world has already been purified, there are no numerous worlds that are not pure.

As stated in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra: "The Buddha-field is as pure as the palace of the sovereign deva," and when the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, the entire trichiliocosm became majestic and pure—is this not the case that if one world is pure, then many worlds are pure?
Because many worlds are pure, it extends in this manner until the very limits of space.

It perfectly encompasses all that exists in the three periods of time—equally pure and immovable. (Because all worlds are purified, it extends through immeasurable and boundless worlds, all of which are uniformly pure and immovable.

"Perfectly encompassing the three periods" refers to the entirety of space and worlds, both vertically and horizontally; it does not refer to the three periods of past, present, and future as perceived by the senses.)
Good son, just as empty space is thus equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable.

Because the four great elements are immovable, you should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable. In this way, up to and including the eighty-four thousand dharani-gates, they are all equal and immovable;
you should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable. (Regarding empty space, the four great elements, and all dharmas:)
All things merge into a single level, completely devoid of any sign of movement. You should know that the nature of awareness is likewise so.
Good son, because the nature of awareness is pervasive, pure, immovable, and perfectly boundless, you should know that the six sense faculties are pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
Because the faculties are pervasive, you should know that the six sense objects are pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. Because the objects are pervasive...
Know that the four great elements pervade the Dharma-realm. In this way, even up to the gates of dhāraṇī, they pervade the Dharma-realm.

(Regarding "perfectly boundless": the nature of awakening is complete and vast, without limit. Since this nature pervades the Dharma-realm, it is the same for the faculties, objects, and the four great elements.

Good son, because that wondrous nature of awakening pervades all, the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are neither destroyed nor mixed. Because the faculties and objects are not destroyed, thus...

Even up to the gates of dhāraṇī, there is neither destruction nor confusion. (The wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment pervades the Dharma-realm; thus, the nature of all phenomena—the faculties and their objects—is like empty space, without mutual defilement or attachment.

Therefore, there is nothing that can be transformed or destroyed, nor anything that can be mixed. It is like hundreds of thousands of lamps illuminating a single room: their light fills the space entirely, without destruction or confusion.
(The light of the lamps represents the natures of the faculties, objects, and so forth; the single room represents the boundless Dharma-realm.)
Good son, because of the perfection of awakening, you should know that a bodhisattva is neither bound by dharmas nor seeks liberation from dharmas.

(The full clarity and brilliance of the nature of awakening is called "perfection"; regarding all dharmas, there is neither bondage nor liberation. One does not loathe birth-and-death, nor does one crave nirvāṇa. (Since awakening has been perfected, one knows that both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like flowers in the sky;

therefore, there is nothing to loathe and nothing to crave. One does not revere those who uphold the precepts, nor does one hate those who violate them. (The nature of awakening is fully luminous, clearly illuminating all objects, just as the light of the eye...)

To clearly understand the objects before one is to have no hatred toward them. One does not value long-standing practice nor disparage a beginner. Once awakening is perfected, one views all learners with equality and without duality;

therefore, one does not place extra weight on those with long-standing habits, nor does one treat new students with neglect. This is like Confucius, who suppressed and instructed Zi Lu when he had ascended to the hall, yet welcomed and advanced the young boy who had purified himself.

Why is this? Because everything is awakening. (In these eight cases, there is neither hatred nor love, for everything is awakening. It is, for example, like the light of the eye clearly perceiving the objects before it.

That light is perfect and complete, free from both aversion and attachment. (The nature of awakening is perfectly luminous; it illuminates all objects just as the visual faculty clearly perceives the objects before one. This is because its radiance is perfect and fully endowed.
Thus, one attains a sudden, comprehensive vision in which there is nothing to be either disliked or loved. Why is this? Because the essence of light is non-dual and devoid of aversion or attachment.
(The visual faculty and the light of awakening share the same empty essence and are likewise free from aversion and attachment; therefore, they may be used as a metaphor.)
"Good son, when these bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age cultivate this mind and achieve its perfection, there is herein neither cultivation nor achievement.
(Once the cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment is perfected, one realizes that originally there was nothing to be cultivated, nor anything to be attained.

Perfect Enlightenment shines universally; (the radiance of Perfect Enlightenment pervades the Dharma-realm. It is quiescent and extinguished, without duality; (quiescence means the absence of thought; extinction means the absence of signs. The pure source is profoundly still and eternally one. Within this, a hundred..."

There are *koṭi-nayuta-asaṃkhyeya* [worlds]—(the *Tripiṭaka* states: *a* means "none," and *saṃkhyeya* means "number"; taken together, this means "innumerable")—as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River (*gaṅgānadīvāluka*).

(The "grains of sand in the Ganges" refers to all the sand within the Ganges River; the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The Ganges itself is already immeasurable, how much more so its sands? This serves as a metaphor for the fact that within the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), there are such innumerable Buddha-lands.

They arise and perish in disarray like flowers in the sky. (All Buddha-worlds are fundamentally without the characteristic of abiding; they are like flowers in the sky that arise and vanish according to conditions.)

(They cease accordingly). Neither identical nor separate. (Regarding the arising and ceasing of the manifested worlds as impermanent: from the beginning, they are neither identical to Perfect Enlightenment nor are they remote from Perfect Enlightenment; all exist within the Great Perfect Enlightenment and cannot be discussed in terms of separation or identity).

Without bondage and without liberation. (Since there is originally nothing to be bound, what could there be in liberation?). Only then does one know that sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning.

(When cultivation and realization reach this point, having already attained the fruit of Buddhahood, one then knows the original nature of sentient beings and sees them as manifest Buddhas). Birth and death, and nirvana, are like a dream from yesterday. (Having known the original nature and seen it as manifest Buddhahood...).
Only then does one realize that the birth and death of delusion and the nirvana after awakening are both like matters occurring within a dream.

Good son, because they are like a dream from yesterday, you should know that birth and death, as well as nirvana, have neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going. (Since birth and death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday, how could there be any characteristics of arising, ceasing, coming, or going?
That which is realized is without gain or loss, without grasping or abandoning. (The Perfect Enlightenment that is realized is originally one's own nature; since it cannot be attained...)

It is thus attained; yet it cannot be attained and lost. Since it cannot be attained and grasped, it also cannot be attained and abandoned). One who is able to realize this has no activity and no cessation, no indulgence and no extinction.
(One who can realize Perfect Enlightenment has no mind of active effort, no mind of cessation, no mind of passive compliance with spontaneity, and no mind of ultimate quiescence.

To possess these four minds constitutes the four illnesses). Within this realization, there is neither subject nor object. (There is no wisdom that realizes, and no characteristic that is realized). Ultimately, there is no realization, nor is there anyone who realizes.
(There is originally no dharma to be realized, nor is there any person who realizes it. The nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.

(When one cultivates and realizes perfect enlightenment to the point where both person and dharma are forgotten, then the nature of all faculties, objects, and dharmas is likewise equal and non-dual, never changing or decaying. Good son, those bodhisattvas practice in this manner.
In this way, through gradual progression, such reflection, such maintenance, such skillful means, and such awakening,
he sought such a Dharma and remained neither confused nor distressed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"O Puyan, you should know: All sentient beings— Their bodies and minds are all like illusions;
The body's form belongs to the four great elements, And the mind-nature returns to the six sense objects. The substance of the four great elements is each separate."
Who is the one who brings about this union? By practicing in this way gradually, all things become entirely pure, unmoving, and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
There is no acting, no ceasing, no striving, and no extinguishing; nor is there anyone capable of realizing it.
All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky; the three periods of time are entirely equal.
Ultimately there is no coming or going; bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, as well as sentient beings of the final age who wish to enter the Buddha-way, should practice in this manner.
Then, within the great assembly, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet with his head, and circumambulated him to the right.
He circumambulated [the Buddha] three times, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, you have skillfully proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the Tathāgata’s pure Great Dharani of Perfect Enlightenment—the dharma-practice of the causal stage and its gradual expedients—thereby awakening and dispelling the ignorance of all sentient beings.
The assembly of dharmic followers present here, having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, [realize that all things are like] illusions..."

All obscurations were cleared away, and the eye of wisdom became pure. (This Bodhisattva praised the Buddha for his excellent exposition in the preceding three chapters regarding the gradual expedient means of the Dharma-practice of the causal stage.
"World-Honored One, if all sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning, for what reason do they still possess all ignorance? (This poses the first question.

"If all ignorance has existed in sentient beings from the beginning, by what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata further say that they have been Buddhas from the very beginning? (This poses the second [question].)
(Question: "Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) throughout the ten directions originally attained the Buddha-way, yet later gave rise to ignorance;

when will all Tathāgatas ever again give rise to all afflictions? (This is the third question posed. "Ordinary beings throughout the ten directions" refers to the various classes of sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions.

"I only pray that you will not abandon your unobstructed great compassion and reveal the secret treasury for the sake of all Bodhisattvas. (To "reveal the secret treasury" means to open and explain the secret words of the Buddha. Its wondrous meaning is vast and boundless...)
...is exhausted; therefore it is called a "Treasury" (pitaka).

Furthermore, for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age who may hear such a sūtra teaching—a dharma-gate of definitive meaning (nītārtha) [specifically referring here to the single sūtra of the *Complete Enlightenment* (Vajrasamādhi-sūtra)]—may they forever sever doubt and regret, and forever be free from a mind of hesitation or remorse.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again after each completion.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the profound secrets and ultimate skillful means.
This is the supreme instruction for all bodhisattvas, the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna, which enables those who practice throughout the ten directions..."
May the Bodhisattvas in training and all sentient beings of the final age attain resolute faith and forever sever doubt and regret.
Listen attentively now; I shall speak for your sake. At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, having received these instructions, rejoiced, and together with the great assembly, listened in silence.

"Good son, throughout all worlds, there is beginning and end, arising and ceasing, before and after, existence and non-existence, gathering and dispersing, starting and stopping (The *Enlightened Awareness Great Commentary* states:

'Initial transformation is the beginning; ultimate realization is the end. Arising anew at every moment is called birth; falling away and perishing at every thought is called cessation. The past is called 'before'; the future is called 'after. The present abiding kalpa is called 'existence'; the empty kalpa is called 'non-existence. The kalpa of formation is called 'gathering';
