Not yet awakened, one practices through the power of illusion (because one has not yet attained awakening, one practices Perfect Enlightenment by means of various illusory powers).

At that time, there are twenty-five kinds of pure wheels of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). These twenty-five wheels consist of the three contemplations of *śamatha*, *samāpatti*, and *dhyāna*; they may be practiced individually, simultaneously, sequentially, or intermittently.

Whether cultivated sequentially or perfected simultaneously, there are twenty-five names in total. As for what is called the "Pure Wheel of Samādhi," it is because the nature of awakening is untainted, capable of transforming all phenomena and crushing all illusions.

If a bodhisattva grasps only extreme tranquility and, by the power of that tranquility, permanently severs the afflictions and achieves ultimate perfection— (grasping solely the single dharma of the profound stillness of *śamatha*,
permanently severing ignorance and finally attaining accomplishment)— and enters *nirvāṇa* without rising from their seat— (that is, realizing extinction right where they sit,

indicating that they do not depend on the cultivation of other dharmas)— this bodhisattva is said to be one who practices *śamatha* alone (this refers to practicing meditative quiescence exclusively).
If Bodhisattvas contemplate all things as being like illusions, then by the power of the Buddha, they transform worlds and perform various activities,

fully practicing the pure and wondrous conduct of a Bodhisattva (because they observe that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, their transformative activities give rise to the wondrous practice of samāpatti).
Within the dhāraṇī of Perfect Enlightenment, they do not lose the tranquil mindfulness of dhyāna nor the various still wisdoms of śamatha.
This is his stillness and wisdom). This Bodhisattva practices only *samāpatti* (this is the exclusive cultivation of the contemplation of illusion).

If these Bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions and do not grasp at their functional manifestations, but instead sever afflictions alone, then once the afflictions are completely severed, they realize the true reality (*tathatā*).

(They desire only to eliminate all illusions and do not grasp at the functional manifestations of *samāpatti*; they exclusively use the tranquil contemplation of *dhyāna* to sever ignorance, thereby realizing the markless mark of Perfect Enlightenment).
This bodhisattva practices *dhyāna* alone (this refers to the exclusive cultivation of quiescent contemplation).
If these bodhisattvas first attain ultimate stillness, they use the mind of still wisdom to illuminate all illusions; therein, they...

They give rise to the bodhisattva practices. This bodhisattva is one who first cultivates śamatha and subsequently cultivates samāpatti (first taking up the ultimate stillness of śamatha, hence "first cultivation"; subsequently initiating the wondrous practice of samāpatti, hence "subsequent cultivation").
If bodhisattvas, by means of the tranquility of wisdom, realize the nature of stillness, they then sever the afflictions and forever transcend birth and death.

Such a bodhisattva is said to have first practiced *śamatha* and subsequently practiced *dhyāna*. (Because they first realize through the tranquility of wisdom in *śamatha*, it is called "first practice";
because they subsequently sever the afflictions and transcend birth and death through *dhyāna*, it is called "subsequent practice.")

If Bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, further manifest various transformations through the power of illusion to deliver sentient beings, and subsequently sever their afflictions to enter into extinction—such Bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha*, then cultivated *samāpatti* in the midst [of that], and finally cultivated *dhyāna*.

(Because they possess the tranquil wisdom of *śamatha* beforehand, it is called "first cultivation"; because they manifest the illusory power of *samāpatti* in the midst [of that process], it is called "in the midst.")
[He] practices [this], and subsequently enters the quiescence of *dhyāna* (hence the phrase "subsequent practice").
If all Bodhisattvas, by the power of ultimate stillness, sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), they thereafter initiate the pure and wondrous conduct of a Bodhisattva.
To deliver all sentient beings—this Bodhisattva is said to first practice *śamatha*, then practice *dhyāna* in the middle, and finally practice *samāpatti*.

(Because there was previously the power of stillness from *śamatha*, it is called "first practice"; because one cuts off and exhausts afflictions through *dhyāna* in the middle, it is called "middle practice";
and because one subsequently gives rise to the wondrous conduct of *samāpatti*, it is called "final practice.")

If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness (*śamatha*), sever afflictions with the mind and further deliver sentient beings while establishing worlds, these Bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and to be simultaneously cultivating *samāpatti* and *dhyāna*.

(Because they possess the power of stillness from *śamatha* beforehand, it is called "first cultivated. When severing and extinguishing afflictions within *dhyāna*, they employ the illusory practices of *samāpatti* to establish worlds; therefore, it is called "simultaneously cultivated.")
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of extreme stillness (*śamatha*), brings forth transformations and subsequently cuts off afflictions (*kleśa*),

this bodhisattva is said to practice *śamatha* and *samāpatti* simultaneously and then practice *dhyāna* afterwards (first using the power of stillness from *śamatha* to assist in bringing forth the transformations of *samāpatti*,
hence "simultaneous practice"; then using *dhyāna* to eliminate afflictions, hence "practice afterwards").
If Bodhisattvas employ the power of ultimate stillness (*śamatha*) to support quiescence (*nirvāṇa*), and subsequently initiate activity to transform worlds,

such Bodhisattvas are said to "cultivate *śamatha* and *dhyāna* simultaneously and then cultivate *samāpatti* later" (meaning they first use the power of stillness from *śamatha* to assist the quiescence of *dhyāna*,
hence "simultaneous cultivation"; subsequently they initiate the activity of *samāpatti* to transform worlds, hence "cultivation later").

If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, accord with various conditions to attain ultimate stillness, such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivated *śamatha*.
(Because they first accord with [conditions] through the illusory power of *samāpatti*, it is called "first cultivation";
because they subsequently attain the ultimate stillness of *śamatha*, it is called "subsequent cultivation.")

If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, attain cessation through various objective realms, such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivated *dhyāna*.
(Because they possess the illusory power of *samāpatti* beforehand, it is called "first cultivation";
because they subsequently attain the cessation of *dhyāna*, it is called "subsequent cultivation.")
If bodhisattvas perform buddha-work through the power of transformation, abiding in tranquility while severing afflictions,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *samāpatti*, then cultivated *śamatha*, and finally cultivated *dhyāna*.

(First, one performs Buddha-work through the illusory power of samāpatti; hence it is called "first cultivation. In the middle, one abides in the tranquility of śamatha; hence it is called "middle cultivation. Finally, one eradicates afflictions through the path of cessation in dhyāna;
hence it is called "final cultivation.")
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation and unimpeded activity, sever the afflictions and abide in ultimate tranquility,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *samāpatti*, then cultivated *dhyāna*, and finally cultivated *śamatha*.

(First, by means of the illusory power of samāpatti, there is unimpeded functioning; hence it is called "initial cultivation. In the middle, by means of the path of the quiescence of dhyāna, one cuts off afflictions; hence it is called "middle cultivation. Finally, one abides in the ultimate stillness of śamatha;
hence it is called "final cultivation.")
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation and skillful application, accord with both supreme stillness and tranquil extinction,

such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated samāpatti while simultaneously cultivating śamatha and dhyāna (because they first employ the illusory power of samāpatti through skillful application,

it is called "first cultivation"; subsequently, they cultivate in accordance with both the supreme stillness of śamatha and the tranquil extinction of dhyāna, hence it is called "simultaneous cultivation").
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, give rise to various activities to support ultimate stillness and subsequently sever the afflictions,
such bodhisattvas are said to practice samāpatti and śamatha simultaneously,

followed by dhyāna (the former refers to using the illusory power of samāpatti to give rise to various activities to support the ultimate stillness of śamatha, hence "simultaneous practice"; the latter refers to severing the afflictions through the path of cessation in dhyāna, hence "subsequent practice").

If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), augment their state of cessation (*śamatha*) and subsequently abide in pure, effortless meditative concentration (*anabhisaṃskāra-dhyāna*),
such bodhisattvas are said to "practice samāpatti and dhyāna simultaneously,

followed by śamatha" (meaning they first use the illusory power of *samāpatti* to augment the cessation of *dhyāna*, hence "simultaneous practice"; subsequently, through *śamatha*, they abide peacefully in pure, non-arising stillness, hence "subsequent practice").

If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of cessation (*nirodha*), gives rise to supreme tranquility and abides in purity, this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *dhyāna* and subsequently cultivated *śamatha*.
(Because there was previously the power of the cessation of *dhyāna*, it is said that one first cultivates and subsequently gives rise to the supreme tranquility of *śamatha*.)
Abiding in purity, it is therefore said that they cultivate [it] subsequently).
If bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence, give rise to functional activity, their quiescence and activity will be in accord with all objects.
This bodhisattva is one who first cultivates dhyāna and subsequently cultivates samāpatti (first cultivating because they already possess the power of the quiescence of dhyāna;
subsequently cultivating because they give rise to the functional activity of samāpatti to accord with all things).
If these bodhisattvas, by means of the power of quiescence, abide in meditative concentration through various intrinsic natures and give rise to transformations,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha* within *dhyāna* and subsequently cultivated *samāpatti*.

(First there is the power of dhyāna and cessation; therefore it is called "prior cultivation. In the middle, various self-natures rest within the meditative concentration of śamatha; therefore it is called "middle cultivation. Finally, the transformations of samāpatti arise;
therefore it is called "subsequent cultivation.")

If Bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation (*śamatha*), through the unconditioned intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), give rise to functional activity within a pure realm and return to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), such Bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *dhyāna*, then practiced *samāpatti* in the middle, and finally practiced *śamatha*.

(Because they previously possessed the power of the cessation of *dhyāna*, it is called "first practice. In the middle, from the unmoving intrinsic nature, they give rise to the functional activity of *samāpatti*; therefore, it is called "middle practice. Finally...
The pure realm returns to the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of *śamatha*; therefore, it is said that "one subsequently cultivates" it.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of cessation, abide in meditative absorption that is variously purified, they give rise to emanations.

This Bodhisattva is named "One Who First Cultivates Dhyāna and Then Cultivates Samatha and Samāpatti" (meaning that because he first possesses the power of the cessation of dhyāna, it is said he "first cultivates";
subsequently, he abides in the meditative concentration of samatha and gives rise to the transformations of samāpatti, hence it is said he "cultivates them together").
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*), augment ultimate stillness and then give rise to transformations,

these bodhisattvas are said to "practice *dhyāna* and *śamatha* simultaneously and subsequently practice *samāpatti*" (meaning they first use the power of *dhyāna*-cessation to augment the ultimate stillness of *śamatha*,
hence "simultaneous practice"; and subsequently give rise to the transformations of *samāpatti*, hence "subsequent practice").

If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*), support their transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) and give rise to the wisdom of an utterly tranquil and lucid realm, such bodhisattvas are said to practice *dhyāna* and *samāpatti* simultaneously and subsequently practice *śamatha*.

(Because they first use the power of the cessation of *dhyāna* to support the transformations of *samāpatti*, it is called "simultaneous practice. Because they subsequently give rise to the ultimate tranquility of *śamatha*, it is called "subsequent practice. As for "the wisdom of a lucid realm," within that ultimate tranquility, both the object and the cognition are pure.

Furthermore), if all Bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, perfectly integrate with all things (that is, they perfectly encompass all phenomena through the wisdom within the nature of perfect enlightenment),

then regarding all natures and characteristics, there is nothing that departs from the nature of enlightenment (since they have perfectly integrated with all things, then amidst all various natures and characteristics, none depart from the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment). These Bodhisattvas...

This is called the "Perfect Cultivation" (yuanxiu) that accords with the three kinds of self-nature purity. (Cultivating the three contemplations simultaneously is what constitutes Perfect Enlightenment).
Good son, these are called the twenty-five wheels of the Bodhisattva. All Bodhisattvas practice in this manner. (The practices of Bodhisattvas do not exceed these twenty-five wheels).

The Tang dynasty monk Weiqiao took these twenty-five wheels and established them as twenty-five contemplations: the first is named "Clarifying the Turbulent and Ceasing Function" (Chenghun xiyong guan); the second is "The Cook Ding Exercising His Blade" (Baoding ziren guan); the third is "Manifesting Sound and Bringing Forth... If bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon this wheel, they should maintain pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), practice tranquil contemplation, and engage in careful reflection.
(To maintain pure conduct means to uphold the Buddha’s precepts; to be tranquil means to clarify one's own mind; and to reflect means to examine what is erroneous and what is correct.)
Seek compassion through repentance for twenty-one days (fearing that the power of karma might obscure the pure mind, one seeks compassion and repents, taking twenty-one days as the period).
At each of the twenty-five wheels, place a marker. With a sincere heart, seek compassion and grasp whichever wheel falls into your hand (like drawing lots; there must be no choosing).

By classifying according to the fetters, one comes to know the sudden and gradual approaches. (The classification of attaining the aforementioned single cultivation of the three wheels or the perfect cultivation of the one wheel constitutes the Sudden Gate; the classification of attaining the remaining twenty-one wheels constitutes the Gradual Gate).
A single moment of doubt or regret means that [the practice] is not accomplished. (If there is a mind of doubt and regret, the contemplative practice will ultimately not be accomplished).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Vimalacāritra, you should know: The unimpeded and pure wisdom of all bodhisattvas Is born entirely from meditative concentration— Namely, śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna.”
The three dharmas are cultivated both suddenly and gradually; there are twenty-five kinds.
Among all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and those who have practiced throughout the three periods of time, there are none who have not attained Bodhi by means of this dharma.
This excludes only those of sudden enlightenment and those whose minds do not accord with the Dharma—all other Bodhisattvas [attain it through these].
"And for the sentient beings of the final age, they should always uphold this wheel;
by practicing it diligently in accordance with the power of the Buddha’s great compassion, they will before long realize nirvana.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions rose from his seat in the midst of the great assembly and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
He circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, for our sakes you have extensively expounded such inconceivable matters—namely, the previously mentioned twenty-five wheels, all of which are matters beyond thought and beyond comparison.

These twenty-five wheels are the characteristics of the practices on the causal grounds of all Tathāgatas; they are the characteristics of the contemplative practices of the first stage of all Buddhas. You have caused this great assembly to attain what they have never before experienced."

"It is so. (The great assembly heard what they had never heard before; hence it is said: "They attained what they had never before attained. They beheld that the spheres of diligent toil and all the functional efforts of the Tamer throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were, in every respect, like a single thought-moment.

We Bodhisattvas felt profound self-congratulation and comfort. (The great assembly saw for themselves that the functional efforts of their cultivation over vast kalpas were as if occurring within a single thought-moment.
"World-Honored One, if the fundamental nature of this awakened mind is pure, by what cause is it defiled, such that it causes all sentient beings..."

They became bewildered and confused, unable to enter [the teaching]. We only pray that the Tathāgata will extensively awaken us to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena—during delusion, it is generally called "original nature";

after awakening, it is then named *dharmatā*). May this great assembly and the sentient beings of the future age be provided with an eye for the future. (Sentient beings of both the present and the future.)

Having heard the Buddha’s instruction—that until the end of the future, there shall forever be no more delusion—he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Having spoken these words, he made this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, it is well that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such skillful means for the sake of this great assembly and for the sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age."
"Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhakarmāvaraṇa received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.
"Good son, since beginningless time, all sentient beings have, through deluded thoughts, clung to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.

(Sentient beings, from beginningless kalpas, have through deluded attachment falsely conceived of the marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. They recognize these four inversions as the substance of a real self.

(They deludedly take these four marks to be the substance of a real self, not knowing that these four inversions are fundamentally non-existent. From this, there arise the two [emotions] of hatred and love."

The objective realm (viṣaya). (Because one grasps the four characteristics as the substance of the self, one loves what accords with the self and hates what opposes it. Within the substance of falsehood, one further clings to falsehood. (The illusory substance of the four great elements is already false;

to further cling to the four characteristics is to add falsehood upon falsehood. These two falsehoods rely on each other to give rise to the path of false karma. (The "two falsehoods" refer to the four great elements together with the four characteristics.)

Second is mutual causality: because one performs karma and receives retribution, it is called "giving rise to deluded paths of action. Because there is deluded karma, there is deluded perception of transmigration. (Since deluded karma exists, one undergoes saṃsāra; fundamentally there is no saṃsāra, hence it is called "deluded perception.
Those who loathe transmigration perceive nirvāṇa as deluded. (They loathe that saṃsāra and desire to realize nirvāṇa;

fundamentally there is no nirvāṇa, hence it is called "deluded perception. Due to this, they cannot enter pure awakening; it is not that awakening rejects those who seek to enter it. (Because they are obstructed by those deluded perceptions, they are unable to awaken and enter.)

Pure awakening is not something that can be obstructed or barred from entering by those who would reject it; rather, there are various capacities for entry because it is through awakening that sentient beings are able to realize and enter [it].
It is not that awakening comes and enters into the nature of sentient beings. This is as Confucius said: "It is man who can broaden the Way, not the Way that broadens man.

Therefore, whether thoughts are stirred or stilled, they all result in delusion and confusion. Why is this? Because of the beginningless, fundamental ignorance (avidyā) that has arisen from the outset.

They take it as their own master. (That they are deluded and distressed in both motion and stillness is because, since beginningless kalpas, ignorance and false conceptualization have served as their masters.

All sentient beings are born without the eye of wisdom. (From birth until now, they have not seen their own nature; therefore, it is said they are born without the eye of wisdom. The nature of body and mind is entirely ignorance. (Since they lack the eye of wisdom...)
Thus, the four great elements and the five aggregates are all illusory in nature; they are entirely the mind of ignorance and attachment.

It is like a person who would not take their own life (just as sentient beings, through deluded attachment and ignorance, are unwilling to eliminate it, much like people in the world who refuse to commit suicide). Therefore, one should know:

if there is someone who loves me, I accord with them (if there is someone who loves me, I also accord with that object and give rise to a heart of love); if they do not accord with me, then resentment and enmity arise (if they do not accord with that object and give rise to a heart of love, then...).

To be angry at those who oppose one’s own views is to give rise to a mind of hatred and resentment. Because this love-hate duality nourishes ignorance, one’s continuous pursuit of the Way will fail to achieve fruition.
(Various forms of hatred and attachment increase the view of self; as this continues uninterrupted from moment to moment, the realization of the Way becomes ever more difficult).

Good son, what is the mark of self? It refers to that which sentient beings take as realized by their minds. (If the mind of a sentient being has nothing to grasp or realize, it does not cling to the mark of self.

As soon as there is something grasped or realized, one clings to this mind and takes it to be one's own self; therefore, it is called the mark of self). Good son, it is like a person whose hundred joints...

When in a state of equilibrium and suddenly forgetting my body—this refers to when sentient beings have nothing to grasp or realize, they do not know there is a mark of self—the tendons of the four limbs become slack and the methods of nourishment go astray;

yet, with the slightest application of needles or moxa, one becomes aware of the existence of a self. (This is a metaphor for how sentient beings only come to know the mark of self once they have something to grasp or realize.

Therefore, it is through grasping and realization that the substance of the self manifests. (Realization is "my realization" and grasping is "my grasping"; thus, at the moment of grasping and realization, the substance of the self appears. Good son, that mind is...
Even to realize the Tathāgata’s ultimate, thorough knowledge of pure nirvāṇa is entirely the mark of a self (for although one may enter the Buddha’s nirvāṇa,
as long as the mind of self has not been severed, it is likewise entirely the mark of a self).

"Good son, what is the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*)? It refers to those sentient beings whose minds have attained realization. (Regarding the 'mark of a person': they realize that the self is empty and are thus able to refrain from attachment.

Regarding 'whose minds have attained realization': they realize that the mark of a self which was realized is non-existent. Good son, one who realizes there is a self no longer identifies with that self.

Since what is realized is not the self, the realization itself is likewise [not the self]. (Although the mark of a self is non-existent and one no longer clings to it, since the self that was realized is already non-self, then that which is capable of realizing it is also [non-self])."

"It is not the self; the characteristic of 'not-self' is itself the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*). Once awakened, one transcends all who have attained realization, yet all such [attainers] are still the mark of a person.
(If this awakened mind considers itself superior to all those who have realized the self-characteristic, it too is merely the mark of a person.

Good son, even if the mind attains perfect enlightenment to the point that both *nirvāṇa* and the self are considered identical, as long as the mind retains even a slight trace of awakening and exhausts every detail of the realized principle, it is all termed the mark of a person. (Though one may perfectly awaken to the *ātman-nirvāṇa* and fully master all principles...")
This is the principle of realizing the realization. However, if there remains even a hair’s breadth of a mind that seeks awakening, this too is merely the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*).
Good son, what is the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*)? It refers to that which the minds of all sentient beings cannot reach through their own self-realization and awakening.

(Each sentient being gives rise to a distinct mind, each thinking to themselves: "The marks of self (*ātman*) and the marks of person (*pudgala*) that I have previously realized and awakened to do not yet reach this level. They do not know that this mind is precisely the mark of a sentient being. Good son, it is like a person who says, "I am a sentient being.
One should know that when that person speaks of a "sentient being," it is neither the self nor the other.

(This uses the words of another person as a metaphor to illustrate that taking oneself to be the mark of a sentient being is neither the mark of self nor the mark of person. Why is it not the self? Because "I" am the multitude...

That which is born is not the self; how could it be "that"? The self is the sentient being, for that [being] is not the self. (To say it is "not the self" means that since one is a sentient being, one is not the [transcendent] self.
To say it is "not that" means that since one is a sentient being, one is not a person. To say it is "not that self" means it is not the self of that other person.

Good son, all sentient beings, in their realization and awakening, take everything to be the self and the person. (This means they perceive what was previously realized as the mark of the self, and what was previously awakened to as the mark of the person.)

That which is beyond the reach of the marks of self and person—(meaning that one realizes one’s own insight is superior to those two marks of self and person)—yet wherein the realization of existence remains, is called the mark of sentient beings.
(Because the realization within the mind has not yet been forgotten, this mark is so named.)

"Good son, what is the characteristic of life-span (*āyus-lakṣaṇa*)? It refers to that which is perceived by the clear and pure illumination of the minds of all sentient beings—that which is understood by awakening (*bodha*).

(That 'which is understood by awakening' means that when one previously grasped the characteristic of a sentient being, the mind that understood it had not yet ceased. This awakened mind continues in a subtle, uninterrupted succession; because it seeks not to be severed or extinguished, it is called the characteristic of life-span.

All karmic wisdoms cannot see this themselves; it is like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). (All awakened minds are pure karmic wisdoms. However, this wisdom is profound and subtle, unable to see itself. Therefore, from moment to moment, it does not... "
It is severed (yet it is like the life-faculty which cannot be severed). Good son, if the mind perceives all that is awakened as being defilements, [it is severed].

(The radiance of the mind shines forth, and various perceptions are seen within the pure nature; yet these are all but dust and defilement). That which perceives and that which is perceived do not depart from the dust, for both the illuminating mind and the perceiving mind are merely thoughts of dust.
Just as when hot water melts ice, there is no separate ice that knows the ice has melted; so too it is with the persistence of a self and the perception of a self.

To persist in a self is like water becoming ice; to perceive a self is like hot water melting the ice. Although the ice and the water differ, they both return to the same water; there is nothing else that can know the ice has melted. Therefore, the persistence of a self and the perception of a self are identical.
[They] return to the single nature. Apart from this, there is no other knower of my awakening).

Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks. Although they may practice the Way with diligent effort for many kalpas, it will be merely called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta);

One can enter pure awakening. (If one practices while grasping at signs, the more diligent one becomes, the more afflicted one will be; by what means could one awaken and enter pure awakening?

(For those who aspire to the fruit of Buddhahood, extensive learning and hearing are not required; they need only be diligent and energetic in restraining deluded thoughts. I prostrate. As false teachings blaze ever more fiercely, causing all sentient beings to ask: "What kind of person should one seek? Upon what dharma should one rely? What practice should one perform? What illness should one eliminate?
How should one resolve the mind?"—so that those who are like the blind may not fall into wrong views. (The Bodhisattva raised these five questions.)

The Eye. (It enables sentient beings to purify their Dharma-eye and not fear the afflictions of Māra. It causes those sentient beings to attain the Noble Path. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.

Good son, when sentient beings in the final age are about to resolve upon the Great Mind and seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) with the desire to practice, they should seek those who possess all correct knowledge and vision.

Those who give rise to immeasurable and vast minds and draw near to great spiritual friends—desiring to cultivate Perfect Enlightenment (Vajraśekhara)—should select those who possess correct knowledge and correct vision.

One who possesses all correct knowledge and vision is one for whom various forms of knowledge and vision are entirely free from defilement and attachment. Their mind does not dwell upon signs (the person of correct knowledge and vision does not have their mind attached to signs).

They do not cling to the realms of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas (the person of correct knowledge and vision does not mentally adhere to the realms of the two vehicles. The *Chuan Xin Fa Yao* states: "Those who awaken by means of vocal teaching are called Śrāvakas;

Although they manifest within the realm of worldly toil, their minds are ever pure (the person of correct knowledge and vision, though manifesting as a transformation body amidst worldly toil, has never had their mind [become defiled]).

[He] manifests various faults. (This refers to a person of right knowledge and vision who, wishing to employ the same means as sentient beings to gather and transform them, displays various faults and afflictions). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Manifesting the practice of desire while remaining free from all attachments;
manifesting various afflictions while the mind is always pure"—this is it. He praises the holy life (*brahmacarya*) so as not to cause sentient beings to enter into non-discipline.

(Although he manifests various faults and afflictions, he also constantly praises true holy conduct, ensuring that sentient beings do not enter into rituals that do not rely upon the precepts). One who seeks such a person will immediately find him.
One achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. (Those who resolve their minds on practice must seek out such persons of right knowledge and right view to serve as teachers and friends;

Those spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) constantly manifest purity within the four modes of deportment; even when they manifest various faults and afflictions, their minds are free from arrogance.

(Within the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—the spiritual friend constantly manifests pure conduct. Wife and family. (For one who seeks the Dharma, it is not even permissible to cherish or spare one's own body and life, let alone amass wealth, treasures, wives, children, and other external possessions. If, O son of good family...
If one does not give rise to evil thoughts toward that virtuous friend, one will be able to ultimately achieve perfect enlightenment. (All states of doubt are termed "evil thoughts";

"Good son, the sublime Dharma realized by those spiritual friends should be free from the four illnesses. What are the four illnesses?

(In the cultivation and realization of Perfect Enlightenment, one must not give rise to the minds of effort, cessation, acceptance, or extinction; to possess these four states of mind constitutes the four illnesses. The first is the illness of effort.

If there is someone who says, 'I shall perform various practices upon my fundamental mind, desiring to seek Perfect Enlightenment,' that nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not something produced through effort."

Because it is attained through effort, it is called "sickness. (To "perform various practices" means to cultivate all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) practices. Since the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) is not realized by means of the conditioned, it is said that it is "not attained through effort.

The Commentary on the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* also states: "Since this involves fabrication and the arising of mental states, how could it be consistent with non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) and tranquil illumination? Second is the sickness of "indulgence. If there is someone who speaks thus:
"We now do not sever birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), nor do we seek nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa and birth-and-death do not arise..."

To extinguish thoughts; to leave everything as it is, following the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). (This means that if one does not sever saṃsāra, does not seek nirvāṇa, does not give rise to various thoughts, yet also does not extinguish thoughts, but instead follows conditions and leaves the mind as it is, wishing to realize perfect enlightenment—failing to know that the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment cannot be awakened through such reliance on the "leaving-as-it-is" mind—it is therefore said:

"it is not because it exists by mere reliance. The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* also says: "Even if one does not restrict good or evil, this is termed the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This is the third [affliction].

This is a sickness. Furthermore, if there is someone who speaks thus: "I shall now permanently still all thoughts within my own mind and attain the tranquil equanimity of all natures, desiring thereby to seek Perfect Enlightenment (Pariniṣpanna-bodhi)," then because that nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not attained through the union of stilling, it is called a sickness.

(That is to say, it is like seeking to realize Perfect Enlightenment by permanently stilling all thoughts so as to attain the various natures—tranquil, unmoving, equal, and non-dual—without knowing that the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment cannot be reached through the union of a stilled mind. This constitutes a sickness. The *Pariniṣpanna-bodhi Commentary* also says: "How can a mind dwelling in quiescence be in accord with [the truth]? One who is free from these four sicknesses knows purity. (Only when there is no mind of effort, cessation, maintenance, or extinction does one know that the fundamental nature is pure.

Seeds. Since such seeds exist, how could there be liberation? Furthermore, if someone regards an enemy as their own parent, with no duality in mind, they will immediately eliminate all illnesses.
(To view an enemy as a relative, love will be present and all hatred will cease. Regarding all phenomena, the feelings of self and other, or hatred and love, are likewise so.
(Once the mind is equanimous, then within all phenomena, various thoughts of loving oneself and hating others likewise do not exist.)
"Good son, sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) should resolve their minds and speak these words:
'Throughout the entirety of space, I shall cause all sentient beings to enter ultimate perfect enlightenment. (At the very beginning of practice, one should immediately make this vast vow.

Regarding all human characteristics (not clinging to the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, or the mark of life-span), one should thus resolve the mind. In this way, one does not fall into false views. (First, there is no self or other, nor hatred or love;

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Universal Awakening, you should know: In the final age, those sentient beings Who seek a virtuous friend Should seek one who possesses right view, Whose mind is far removed from the Two Vehicles, And who has eliminated the four maladies within the Dharma."
That is to say: practice stopping, abiding, relinquishment, and cessation; draw near to others without pride; remain far removed from anger and resentment;

Do not transgress the non-disciplinary rules; let the root of the precepts be forever pure, and deliver all sentient beings.
Ultimately entering perfect enlightenment, Free from the marks of self, other, and person, Constantly relying on right wisdom,
one immediately transcends false views And realizes awakening and parinirvāṇa. Thereupon,
the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him to the right.
They circumambulated him three times, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, for our sakes you have extensively expounded the various skillful means of Pure Enlightenment, so that sentient beings of the final age may achieve great benefit.

For those who have not yet attained awakening, how should they dwell in summer retreat to cultivate this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment? (Please explain how future sentient beings should abide in and practice this Dharma.

*samāpatti*—the contemplation of illusion; and *dhyāna*—the contemplation of quiescence. We pray that, out of great compassion, you will [instruct] the great assembly and those of the final age.

"To bring great benefit to all sentient beings. Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground. Thus they made this request three times, beginning again and again from the end.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, saying: "Excellent, excellent! O sons of good family, you..."
"You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such skillful means, thereby bestowing great benefit upon all sentient beings. Listen attentively now;
I shall explain it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.

"Good son, whether the Buddha remains in the world, after his parinirvāṇa, or during the final age of the Dharma, there may be sentient beings who possess the nature of the Mahāyāna and believe in the Buddha’s secret, great, perfectly enlightened mind (*mahā-vajra-citta*).

Should such beings wish to practice, whether they are in a *saṃghārāma* (monastery) or dwelling among a community of followers—[those possessing the Mahāyāna nature] being those endowed with the fundamental capacity for Buddhahood; [as for *saṃghārāma*, the Tripitaka states this means "garden of the assembly," referring to the present-day monastic community]..."

[This is] renunciation. Because there are matters involving external conditions, one should reflect and examine according to one's own capacity, as I have already explained. (Since one is constrained by external conditions, one should practice according to one’s own measure.
Furthermore, if there are no other incidental causes or conditions, one should establish a *maṇḍala* and set a time limit.

If a long period is established, it shall be one hundred and twenty days; a medium period, one hundred days; and a short period, eighty days. (The Buddha said that if the days are too long, the ordinary mind easily becomes weary; if the days are too short, [the mind does not reach its potential].)

Because sublime conduct has not yet been perfected, three periods are established as a moderate regulation. One should establish a pure dwelling (establishing the *bodhimaṇḍa* in a clean and pure location).

If the Buddha is currently present, one should engage in right reflection (when the Buddha dwells in the world, one should contemplate with a correct mind, severing all delusive thoughts; the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* also state that the elimination of delusive thoughts constitutes right reflection).

If after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one establishes images and maintains them in the mind and visualizes them with the eyes, generating right mindfulness, this is identical to the constant presence of the Tathāgata.

During the period of dwelling [in practice], those who give rise to right mindfulness—this refers to the state of non-thought. That is to say, even when facing a Buddha image, one should regard it as if the Buddha were actually present; one must not give rise to deluded thoughts.
One should suspend banners and flowers for twenty-one days (the offering of banners and flowers lasts for twenty-one days).

Prostrating to the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, one should seek compassion and repent (sincerely prostrating and chanting the names of the Buddhas, one seeks the Buddhas’ compassionate pity and repents for the three karmas). Upon encountering auspicious signs, one attains mental lightness and tranquility (through the recollection of the Buddha and the practice of repentance).

Thereafter, one may see images of the Buddha, or perceive radiance, or encounter all manner of auspicious objects, whereby the mind attains pliancy and ease. After three weeks have passed, one should continue to maintain focused mindfulness exclusively.

(If more than twenty-one days have passed, do not further recite the Buddha's name or perform repentance; instead, consistently collect and maintain right mindfulness so as not to let it become lax). If the beginning of summer arrives, one should observe the three-month *varṣā* retreat.

One should dwell as a pure Bodhisattva. (If one encounters the beginning of summer, one should immediately enter the summer retreat (*varṣā*). One observes the chamber and does not go out for three months; this is called the "contemplation of the pure dwelling of a Bodhisattva").

The mind is detached from the Śrāvakas, and there is no reliance on a following of disciples. (The *Chuan Xin Fa Yao* says: "Those who attain awakening through vocal teaching are called Śrāvakas. Now that one has entered the summer retreat for pure contemplation, why wait for vocal teaching? Therefore it is said: 'the mind is detached from the Śrāvakas.

Since the mind is already detached from the Śrāvakas, why rely on the assistance of a following of disciples? On the day of the retreat's commencement, one should perform [the ritual] before the Buddha.
Thus he spoke: "I, a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, on this day of pure contemplation during the *anagya*, make this vow before the Buddha.

"I, [Name], mounted upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, practice the path of quiescence" (this refers to personally practicing the sublime conduct according to the Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas). Together we enter...
Abiding in the pure true reality (dharmatā), [all] awaken to and enter the markless within marks, maintaining this state without error. Taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery.

(“Gārala” means a community of the assembly. To now designate Perfect Enlightenment as the Gārala is to clarify that our assembly does not rely upon any other dharma. The body and mind dwell securely in the Wisdom of Equality.

(The body and mind dwell securely within Great Perfect Enlightenment; nature and wisdom merge into a single state of equality. Because the self-nature of Nirvāṇa is without attachment or dependence. (The nature of quiescent extinction is vast and autonomous;
it is neither bound by anything nor subject to any authority. Now I respectfully entreat you: do not follow the Śrāvakas, but together with those of the ten directions...
The Tathāgatas and the great Bodhisattvas observe the three-month *varṣā* retreat for the sake of cultivating the great causal conditions for the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment of a Bodhisattva;
